name: Power and Cooling
blurb: Grid connection, generation, and thermal management.

items.name: Datacenter electricity demand
items.note: DOE's 2024 LBNL report: datacenters consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023, projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028 - AI is the driver

items.name: The liquid-cooling transition
items.note: Blackwell rack systems are liquid-cooled by design; 120kW-class racks ended air cooling's run at the AI high end
items.maker: NVIDIA (GB200 NVL72 as the forcing function)

items.name: PUE and efficiency reporting
items.note: Google publishes fleet-wide power usage effectiveness (trailing twelve-month ~1.1) as the reference efficiency disclosure

reading.body:
U.S. datacenter electricity consumption is on track to nearly triple its share of national demand by 2028, driven explicitly by AI, and the hardware causing that growth now requires liquid cooling as a baseline condition, not an option.

The DOE projection, a range of 6.7 to 12 percent of U.S. electricity by 2028 against 4.4 percent in 2023, is wide enough to signal genuine uncertainty about the pace of AI buildout, but the direction is unambiguous. The forcing function on the cooling side is equally clear: 120kW-class rack systems cannot be managed with air, so liquid cooling is now the default architecture for AI infrastructure, not a premium choice made after the fact.

Efficiency metrics like PUE measure how much overhead power a facility consumes beyond compute itself. A trailing figure near 1.1 represents a mature, well-optimized operation, but PUE does not capture how much raw compute power is being drawn in the first place. High efficiency and rising absolute demand are fully compatible, and the DOE numbers make clear that efficiency gains are not offsetting the aggregate growth in load.

The data covers demand share, cooling architecture, and one operator's efficiency benchmark. It does not address grid capacity, interconnection timelines, or whether the supply side can meet the projected demand range. Those gaps are where the binding constraint actually sits.
